summary: Describes an architecture for IPv6 over the TSCH mode of IEEE 802.15.4. It combines a fast powered backbone with low-power wireless subnetworks that hop channels on a schedule, to give low latency, low jitter, and high reliability.

eli5.summary: Tiny wireless sensors take turns talking on a timetable and hop between channels, so messages arrive reliably and on time.

questions: how does a device join a 6tisch network
subtitle: How IPv6 runs over tiny battery-powered radios that talk on a strict timetable and hop between channels.

tldr.problem: Low-power wireless devices in factories, buildings and meters need IP connectivity with low latency, low jitter and high reliability, which ordinary best-effort wireless does not give.
tldr.mechanism: 6TiSCH puts IPv6, 6LoWPAN and RPL on top of the IEEE 802.15.4 TSCH MAC, adds a 6top sublayer that turns scheduled time-and-channel cells into IP links, and joins several such networks through a fast backbone.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is an Informational architecture that ties together the separate 6TiSCH specifications for joining, scheduling, routing and security, and it also describes Tracks for deterministic paths.

today: RFC 9030 is an Informational RFC published in May 2021, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is the architecture document for the 6TiSCH specifications such as RFC 9031 for joining and RFC 8480 for the 6top Protocol.

sections.title: Introduction and Goals
sections.content:
Wireless links connect many kinds of devices cheaply, even where wiring is impractical. Deterministic Networking aims to maximize the packet delivery ratio within a bounded latency. The RFC lists uses such as industrial automation and control, building automation, in-vehicle control, asset tracking, drones and home automation.

The Time-Slotted Channel Hopping (TSCH) mode of the IEEE 802.15.4 MAC is both time-division and frequency-division multiplexing, so each transmission can use a different channel. It allows transmissions to be scheduled for deterministic operation and suits the slower, most energy-constrained wireless cases.

The 6TiSCH architecture builds an IPv6 multi-link subnet from a federating backbone and a number of TSCH low-power wireless networks. It uses 6LoWPAN to adapt IPv6 to the constrained medium and the Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks (RPL) for distributed routing. It can also support centralized route and schedule computation.
sections.eli5: Some machines need their messages to arrive on time every time. This design gives tiny wireless gadgets a timetable so they do not bump into each other.

sections.title: Subnet Model and Protocol Stack
sections.content:
In the basic configuration a 6TiSCH network is one IPv6 subnet formed by a single Low-Power and Lossy Network (LLN) over a synchronized TSCH mesh. A powered LLN Border Router (6LBR) acts as RPL Root and 6LoWPAN header compression terminator. Because the mesh is non-broadcast multi-access, ordinary IPv6 Neighbor Discovery does not fit, so 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery extends it.

In the extended configuration several LLNs are joined over a backbone that can be wired or wireless. A Routing Registrar that proxies Neighbor Discovery for the nodes is called a Backbone Router (6BBR). The 6BBRs synchronize over the backbone so that the LLNs stay tightly synchronized.

The architecture limits the stack variations. UDP, IPv6 and CoAP are the transport choice instead of TCP and HTTP. 6LoWPAN header compression handles IPv6 and UDP headers, the 6LoWPAN Routing Header compresses RPL artifacts, and OSCORE protects the join protocol and is expected to protect application payloads. Where a deployment does not need all of this, such as RPL in star topologies, it may adopt a subset.
sections.eli5: Small wireless neighborhoods connect to a fast wired road, and special gateways at the edge help them act like one big town.

sections.title: Timeslots, Slotframes and Scheduling
sections.content:
TSCH divides time into timeslots, and each communication opportunity is a cell, identified by a slotOffset and a channelOffset. The Channel Distribution and Usage (CDU) matrix describes the time and frequency layout. Its height is the number of channels and its width is the period of the scheduling operation. Timeslots of 10 to 15 milliseconds are typical, enough for a frame, an acknowledgment and the security check.

A slotframe is a repeating collection of timeslots. A node can run several slotframes with different priorities, typically one for scheduled traffic with the highest precedence and others for RPL traffic. The channelOffset is turned into a real frequency through a hopping sequence that depends on the absolute time, which produces the channel hopping.

The 6top sublayer sits between IP and the TSCH MAC. It gives IP the abstraction of a link made from a pair of bundles of cells, one per direction. A hard cell is managed by an outside scheduler such as a Path Computation Element, while a soft cell can be added, removed or moved by 6top itself using the 6top Protocol (6P) and a Scheduling Function.

Nodes must stay time synchronized, so 6TiSCH uses a RPL instance dedicated to time distribution that keeps the structure loop-free. A node that has not joined it advertises a Join Priority of 0xFF.
sections.eli5: Time is cut into little turns and the radio channels change each turn. Each device is told which turns are its own, so nobody talks over anybody else.

sections.title: Joining, Registration and Schedule Management
sections.content:
A new device is called a pledge. It finds the network from Enhanced Beacons and talks to the Join Registrar/Coordinator (JRC) through a Join Proxy (JP), a radio neighbor that is already part of the network. The join protocol provides mutual authentication, authorization and distribution of parameters over a secure channel. The Constrained Join Protocol (CoJP) does this over OSCORE, and with pre-shared keys the pledge can join after a single round trip with the JRC. After joining, the node gets a network prefix and registers its IPv6 addresses with 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery.

The RFC names four ways to manage the schedule, and not every use case needs all of them. Static scheduling is the only one expected in all implementations.

RPL is used for distributed routing, and the architecture recommends co-locating the 6LBR and the RPL Root so one device has all the information about the attached nodes.
sections.eli5: A new gadget asks a neighbor who is already in the club to introduce it to the club leader. After the leader checks it and gives it a secret key, it can join.

sections.title: Tracks and Forwarding
sections.content:
A Track is a directed path from a source node to one or more destinations across the LLN. It is the 6TiSCH form of a deterministic path from DetNet. Buffers and bundles of cells are reserved along it, so each node knows which bundle to receive from and which to send on. The RFC lists benefits including lower delay from Layer 2 forwarding, guaranteed throughput and maximum latency, energy saving by sleeping in inactive slots, and protection from interference between Tracks.

A Serial Track is a simple chain of paired receive and transmit bundles. A Complex Track is a directed acyclic graph that supports multipath forwarding, so a packet can be replicated over two branches and the duplicate eliminated at the destination. A Track may even extend into a larger DetNet network.

Three forwarding models are supported: classical IPv6 forwarding using the routing table, Track Forwarding that switches a frame at Layer 2 from one timeslot to another regardless of the upper protocol, and 6LoWPAN Fragment Forwarding, where later fragments follow the route set up by the first.
sections.eli5: A Track is a reserved lane through the network, and for important messages it can send two copies down different lanes so one gets through.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Tracks depend on a controller with a Path Computation Element, which must be reachable. If that connection is lost, existing Tracks may keep running until their lifetime ends, but new ones cannot be installed. Communication with the PCE and the JRC must be secured and should be protected against denial of service.

Because the hopping sequence is well known, an attacker who identifies the cell of one flow can jam just that cell at the physical layer without knowing any link-layer keys. This is hard to detect because only one flow suffers. The architecture expects link-layer security to be on at all times, except for the first step of joining.

Time is also a target. The nonce for the link-layer integrity check is built from the source address and the Absolute Slot Number (ASN), and a replayed beacon could give a pledge a stale ASN and open a nonce-reuse attack. The RFC also explains rekeying. It notes that the 2-byte short addresses can run out, and that the ASN wraps after 2^40 timeslot durations, around 350 years with the default values.
sections.eli5: Because the timetable is public, a bully could block one friend's turn, so the network keeps secrets, checks the clock, and changes its keys now and then.

viz.caption: FOUR WAYS TO MANAGE THE SCHEDULE (RFC 9030, SECTION 3.4)

items.title: Static Scheduling
items.text: One fixed schedule for the whole network, used in a Slotted ALOHA fashion. Needed for joining and expected in all implementations.

items.title: Neighbor-to-Neighbor
items.text: Peers add, move and remove cells with 6P under a Scheduling Function.

items.title: Remote Monitoring
items.text: A central controller computes the schedule, with a PCE and a Network Management Entity.

items.title: Hop-by-Hop
items.text: Cells along a path are reserved for a flow using a distributed mechanism.
